title: The Laburnum Top (Poem, Hornbill)

overview.intro: The poem observes a laburnum tree in September: motionless, its leaves yellowing, until a goldfinch arrives at the nest hidden in its trunk and the whole top quivers with feeding and song. The unit studies how Hughes builds stillness before movement, what the phrase the engine of her family does in the middle of the poem, and why the ending returns the tree to silence without letting the reader forget what passed through it.

learningOutcomes: Describe the poem’s movement from stillness to movement and back.
Explain the metaphor of the engine of her family.
Analyse how sound and rhythm enact the poem’s action.
Account for the effect of the return to silence at the end.
Answer poetry extract questions on imagery and structure.

learn.title: The tree before the bird: building stillness

blocks.text: The opening stanzas are given over almost entirely to inaction, and that is the poem’s first technique. The laburnum stands in September with its leaves turning yellow, the seed-pods hanging, and the trunk dark at the centre — a picture with no event in it. Hughes earns the movement that follows by making the reader feel the weight of the quiet: nothing happens for lines at a time, the descriptions are of colour and texture rather than of action, and the stillness is so complete that the arrival of the bird reads as an interruption of something permanent.

The detail matters for what comes next. By establishing the tree as an object — translucent, gold-green, motionless — the poem sets up a contrast between the plant world, which endures quietly, and the animal world, which arrives, works and departs. Examination answers should notice that the stillness is not decorative: it is the condition against which the goldfinch’s energy can register, and it is also what the final stanza restores.

items: September: yellowing leaves, hanging pods, motionless trunk.
The opening stanzas describe texture, not event.
Stillness is built so that movement can be felt as arrival.
The tree is presented as enduring; the bird as transient.
The final stanza returns to exactly this condition.

learn.title: The goldfinch: flicker, feed and the engine of her family

blocks.text: The bird arrives as a flicker of movement — sudden, small and exact — and the poem’s tempo changes with it. She lands, darts, reaches the nest-hole in the trunk, and the young are fed. The descriptions are of quickness: flicker, darting, the quivering of the branch, and the sound she brings with her. What Hughes captures is not a bird seen at rest but a bird working, and the choice of verb throughout insists on labour rather than on charm.

At the centre of the poem stands the metaphor that gives it its argument: the goldfinch is the engine of her family. An engine is the source of power that makes a mechanism run, and by transferring that word to a small bird feeding her young, Hughes converts the nest from a hidden domestic scene into a working machine whose power is the mother’s movement. Everything that trembles in the tree trembles because of her; the stillness the poem opened with turns out to have contained an engine all along, unseen. The image also prepares the ending: an engine can be switched off, and when she flies away the machine stops.

learn.title: The return to silence and what it now means

blocks.text: The final stanza brings back the stillness of the opening, but the return is not a reset, because the reader now knows what the quiet contains. The tree looks as it did, yet the poem has disclosed the family inside it and the energy that passes through it daily, so the silence of the ending reads as a silence of concealment rather than of emptiness. That is the difference between the first page and the last: the same image, and a reader changed by the intervening action.

The technique behind the ending is restraint: Hughes does not moralise about nature’s hidden life or convert the scene into a lesson. The goldfinch simply leaves, the sound stops, and the poem stops with it. The effect — what classroom readings have generally agreed on — is a temporary burst of life followed by a return to stillness, with the implied knowledge that the burst will recur. Answers should avoid presenting any single symbolic reading as the only meaning: the poem supports readings about hidden vitality, about the dependence of the visible world on unseen work, and about the difference between an observer’s stillness and a creature’s labour, and all three should be argued from the images rather than asserted.

items.note: An industrial word transferred to a feeding bird: labour named as power.
Stillness restored, but now legible as concealment of life.

learn.title: Sound, rhythm and how the poem performs its subject

blocks.text: The poem performs its subject in its rhythms. The opening lines move in long, level syllables that make the reading slow, matching the motionless tree; the middle stanzas break into shorter units with harder consonants as the bird flickers and feeds; and the close lengthens again into quiet. The change is audible when the poem is read aloud, and it is the clearest evidence for any answer about how form reflects content.

Imagery is similarly disciplined: the poem stays within colour (gold, green, yellow), movement (flicker, dart, quiver) and sound (trill, song), and refuses metaphor except at the single central point where the engine arrives. That economy is why one metaphor can carry the whole poem. For extract answers, identify the sensory field the quoted lines belong to, note the rhythm of the sentence containing them, and then say where in the poem’s movement the detail sits — stillness, arrival, labour or return.

questions.prompt: How does the poem show the goldfinch’s arrival changing the tree?
questions.answer: Before her arrival the poem describes the tree in terms of colour and texture — yellowing leaves, hanging pods, a motionless trunk — and the reading tempo is slow. When she flickers into view the verbs turn quick and exact: she lands, darts, reaches the nest-hole, and the branch quivers with her movement and her song. The change is therefore shown in three registers at once: action (sudden movement where there was none), sound (trilling where there was quiet), and tempo (shorter, harder rhythms where there had been level lines). The tree itself does not change; what changes is the activity passing through it.
questions.explanation: Three registers of change — action, sound and tempo — with a detail from each are required.

questions.prompt: Explain the phrase the engine of her family.
questions.answer: The phrase works by transferring the vocabulary of machinery to a living bird. An engine is the part of a machine that generates power and makes everything else move, and by calling the goldfinch that, the poet presents the nest inside the trunk as a mechanism and her feeding visits as the power source that keeps it running — hence the trembling branch and the sound, which are the machine in operation. The metaphor also carries a judgement: the activity of the family depends entirely on her labour, and without her arrivals there is no motion at all. Finally it prepares the ending, because an engine can be switched off: when she flies away, the movement stops and the tree returns to stillness, now understood as a stopped mechanism rather than an empty object.
questions.explanation: The explanation must unpack source of power, the nest as mechanism, dependence, and the preparation of the ending.

questions.prompt: How does Hughes move from stillness to movement and back again? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The poem is built as a deliberate excursion from quiet into energy and out again, and its structure can be traced stanza by stanza. The opening establishes stillness as the normal condition of the tree: September light, leaves going translucent, seed-pods hanging, the trunk dark and untroubling, and the sentences long and level so that reading itself is slowed. The arrival of the goldfinch breaks the pattern physically and prosodically — the flicker, the dart, the quiver of the branch — and the lines shorten as the action quickens, so the reader experiences speed rather than being told about it. The centre of the excursion is the engine metaphor, where the poem states its argument: the stillness had concealed a powered family, and the labour of one bird makes the whole top move. Her departure then reverses everything — the sound stops, the trembling ceases, the tree stands as before — but the reversal is not a return to innocence, because the reader now reads the silence as concealment. That is the poem’s achievement in miniature: identical images at the beginning and the end, and a reader changed in between. The answer should quote one detail from each movement and note the tempo of each, because the structural argument and the rhythm argument are the same argument in this poem.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the four movements traced with quotations and the point that the closing stillness means differently from the opening.

questions.prompt: Does the poem celebrate hidden life, or simply record what the poet saw? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case for recording rests on the poem’s precision and its refusal of commentary. Every detail is observational — the month, the yellowing leaves, the seed-pods, the exact behaviour of a feeding bird — and the diction belongs to natural description rather than to sentiment: no emotion is named, no comparison is drawn between the bird’s life and human life, and even the poem’s one large metaphor, the engine, is technically apt rather than ornamental, because it describes how the nest’s activity is powered. The ending reinforces the restraint: the bird flies, the tree is still, the poem stops, with no lesson appended. Read this way the poem belongs to the tradition of the carefully watched nature lyric, where accuracy is the whole achievement. The case for celebration rests on what the watching reveals. The poem’s movement is not neutral: it withholds the nest from the reader just as the tree withholds it from a passer-by, and when the discovery comes it is presented as an event — a burst of movement, sound and life in a scene that had appeared inert. The engine metaphor is an act of emphasis, elevating a feeding bird to the status of power source, and the final silence is composed to be felt rather than merely noted, since the reader cannot now look at the still tree without imagining what it hides. The poem thus argues that stillness is an appearance and unseen labour sustains the visible world — a claim, not an observation. The balanced judgement is that observation is the method and revelation the result: Hughes records precisely so that the record itself discloses something, and the poem’s honesty lies in never stepping outside the seen to state the meaning. The best answers will quote from both the descriptive opening and the emphatic centre, and show that the celebration is carried entirely by selection and ordering rather than by declared feeling.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both cases evidenced, the observation that the ending is composed rather than accidental, and a judgement about how selection produces meaning without statement.
